turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?
turns.patient_response:
Well, to be honest, it was mostly my wife’s idea, and my supervisor at the plant kind of pushed for it too. What brought me in is... well, people just keep saying I’m not listening to them. It’s happening all the time now and it's causing a lot of friction. 

Like, I work in production, right? So my supervisor will come up to my station, look me dead in the eye, and start talking straight to me about a change in the line or whatever we're doing that shift. And I’m looking right back at him, I swear I am, but then a minute later he walks off and I realize I only caught maybe half of it. So then I have to go track him down and ask him to say it all over again, which obviously really ticks him off because we're on a tight schedule. 

And it’s the exact same story at home. My wife will be sitting right across from me at the kitchen table, talking straight to me about her day or the bills or whatever, and I'm nodding along, but suddenly I realize my brain was just somewhere else entirely and I missed a huge chunk of what she just said. I have to stop her and ask her to repeat herself, and she gets so mad because she thinks I just don't care or I'm ignoring her on purpose. But I do care! It's just... I don't know, it's like the words just slip right past me, and I'm tired of everyone being mad at me for it.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly describes frequently failing to process or hear what is being said when spoken to directly by their supervisor and wife, requiring them to repeat themselves.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have trouble hearing other sounds, like the TV, phone, or conversations in a noisy room?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, my hearing is actually perfect. It's funny you ask that, because my wife actually thought the exact same thing a couple years back. She was convinced I was going deaf, so she actually made me go to the urgent care clinic to get my ears flushed out, thinking it was wax build-up or something. But the nurse looked in there and said my eardrums were pristine, absolutely nothing wrong. 

And at the plant, you know, we have to do those annual hearing tests because of OSHA regulations. The stamping presses I work near get incredibly loud, so we have to wear the heavy-duty ear protection, but they still make us go into that little soundproof booth with the headphones every year and click the button when we hear the little beeps. I pass with flying colors every single time. Top of the charts for my age, the safety guy tells me. 

I can hear the TV perfectly fine, and I can hear my phone buzzing in my pocket even when I'm driving a forklift on the noisy side of the floor. Honestly, sometimes I feel like I hear *everything* going on in a noisy room, like every little side conversation and machine humming and all of it at once. So it’s definitely not my ears. The sound gets in just fine, it's just... I don't know, once it gets past my ears, my brain just doesn't record the actual message. But physically hearing things? No, no problem at all.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient notes that while their physical hearing is fine, their 'brain just doesn't record the actual message,' confirming the cognitive aspect of not listening when spoken to.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes hearing 'every little side conversation and machine humming and all of it at once' in a noisy room, indicating high responsiveness to extraneous stimuli.

turns.doctor_question: Do you also have this same problem of drifting off or missing what people say when you’re at home, at work, and in other parts of your life?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, it's everywhere. It's not just one place, it's... it's really affecting my whole life right now. Like at work, it’s gotten incredibly serious. I mean, it used to just be my supervisor getting annoyed and pulling me aside, but now I’ve actually had formal warnings. Like, actual written warnings that go straight into my HR file. And that terrifies me, to be honest with you, because I really worry I could lose my job over this. Or worse, you know, working in production with all those heavy stamping presses and conveyors... if I drift off and miss a safety update during the morning shift huddle, I could cause a major safety problem on the line. Someone could get seriously hurt, or lose a finger, all because my brain decided to check out when they were explaining a new lockout-tagout procedure. I just can't have that on my conscience, and I definitely can't afford to be unemployed at my age. 

And then I go home, hoping to just leave the stress behind, but it’s the exact same story there. My wife and my kids... they just get so incredibly frustrated with me. My wife tries so hard to keep the house running on a tight schedule, especially with the kids' school stuff and trying to get everyone fed, but instead of helping things run smoothly, I just end up disrupting all their routines. Like, she’ll tell me exactly what she needs me to do to help get the kids out the door, and I just totally miss it or zone out, and then I'm doing something completely unhelpful while everyone else is scrambling. Next thing I know, we're late, the kids are stressed, my wife is furious because I derailed the whole morning... I just feel like I'm a wrench in the gears everywhere I go, you know? It never stops.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes their brain 'checking out' and 'drifting off' during explanations and meetings at work, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient admits to totally missing it or zoning out when their wife speaks directly to them to tell them what to do.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient fails to follow through on their wife's instructions for morning routines, ending up doing something completely unhelpful instead.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar problems paying attention or daydreaming when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, yeah. Yeah, absolutely. It’s funny you ask about being a kid, because honestly, this isn't exactly new for me. I mean, it’s worse now, or maybe the consequences are just bigger now with the job and the kids, but... yeah, I was exactly like this back then, too. 

I remember elementary school was just a constant struggle. My mom used to have these huge stacks of report cards and notes from teachers, and it was always the same thing. They were always moving my desk. Like, every other week it felt like I was being relocated. First I’d be in the back, then I’d be up right next to the teacher's desk, then they’d put me off by the window, hoping I guess that if I was isolated I wouldn't be such a problem. But the thing was, I just... I couldn't stay put. I’d be up sharpening my pencil three times during a math lesson, or I’d drop my eraser just so I could crawl under the desk to get it, or I'd just be standing up at my seat without even realizing I'd stood up. 

And the talking... oh man, the talking. I was always getting my name on the board for blurting things out. The teacher would ask a question, and before she even finished the sentence, I’d just shout out the answer. I didn't even think to raise my hand, it was like the thought went from my brain straight out of my mouth with zero filter. And it wasn't just with the teachers, either. I was always getting into trouble for butting into other kids' business. Like, if the kid next to me was doing a worksheet and I saw they were stuck, I’d just reach over and start doing it for them, or I'd grab their crayons, or I'd just start talking to them while we were supposed to be doing silent reading. 

All of this was happening way before middle school, you know? Like second, third, fourth grade. My mom was always getting called in for parent-teacher conferences because I was just... I was exhausting for them, I think. I just couldn't sit still and I couldn't keep my mouth shut, and I was always in someone else's space. So, yeah, the daydreaming and the not paying attention and all that... it's been going on for as long as I can remember, really. It just looked a little different back then when I was a kid bouncing off the walls of a classroom instead of a grown man zoning out at a stamping press.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms having problems with daydreaming and not paying attention since childhood.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient states he had a major problem with talking in class and 'couldn't keep my mouth shut'.
